alignment.note: Greek opens with the coordinating conjunction Καί ('and') governing a genitive absolute; the Vulgate splits this into Et + cum, introducing a subordinate temporal clause (cum ... esset), while the Peshitta uses the single subordinating particle ܟܕ ('when'). The three traditions express the same temporal frame through different syntactic strategies.

Greek employs a genitive absolute (ὀψίας γενομένης, 'evening having come'); the Vulgate renders it as a finite subjunctive clause (sero esset); the Peshitta uses a finite verb ܗܘܐ with the postpositive particle ܕܝܢ ('but/now') and the noun ܪܡܫܐ ('evening'). The Syriac ܕܝܢ has no counterpart in the Greek or Latin and functions as a discourse connective rather than a strict translation.

Greek uses the simple imperfect ἦν ('was'); the Vulgate matches with erat; the Peshitta employs a periphrastic construction ܐܝܬܝܗ ܗܘܬ (enclitic 'it is' + auxiliary 'was'), a characteristic Syriac means of expressing durative or stative past, semantically equivalent to the Greek imperfect.

Greek has the articular noun τὸ πλοῖον ('the boat'); the Vulgate navis and the Peshitta ܣܦܝܢܬܐ lack a definite article (Latin having none and Syriac expressing definiteness via the emphatic state), so the determination is conveyed morphologically rather than by a separate token.

ἐν μέσῳ τῆς θαλάσσης / ܡܨܥܬ ܝܡܐ / in medio mari — 'in the midst of the sea.' The Greek and Latin use a prepositional phrase with the genitive/ablative, while the Peshitta uses the construct noun ܡܨܥܬ governing ܝܡܐ, all semantically identical.

καὶ αὐτός / ܘܗܘ / et ipse — 'and he himself.' The Peshitta fuses the conjunction ܘ and the independent pronoun ܗܘ into a single graphic unit, whereas Greek and Latin keep conjunction and pronoun separate.
μόνος / ܒܠܚܘܕܘܗܝ / solus — 'alone.' The Syriac form carries a third masculine singular pronominal suffix ('by himself'), but this is idiomatic and does not constitute a semantic divergence.

Greek ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς and Latin in terra denote 'upon the land,' using γῆ/terra. The Peshitta ܥܠ ܐܪܥܐ uses ܐܪܥܐ ('earth/land'), the standard Syriac equivalent; the slight lexical-semantic range ('earth' vs. 'dry land') is a routine rendering difference with no doctrinal weight.
